heatbud-el-nino.linkedin:
For weeks, everyone was talking about El Niño. Hotter months. Heavier afternoons.

And I was too busy to notice any of it.

I'd look up mid-afternoon with a headache, see my water bottle still full, and only then realise how hot it had become.

Weather apps gave me a number. None of them told me what to do with it. When is it safe to step out? How much water do I actually need today?

So I designed and built HeatBud ☀️

→ It shows how hot it really feels, not just the air temperature
→ It tells you the safest time to go out, in one plain sentence
→ It gives you a daily water plan based on your body, your routine and the forecast
→ And it comes with a little buddy, because heat is serious but it shouldn't feel scary

I work indoors. Millions of Nigerians don't. Riders, traders, builders, students walking to class. They're who I want this to help most.

It's live, works on any phone, and I'm still improving it.

Try it: heatbud.netlify.app

ai-designs-everywhere-consulting.linkedin:
A founder sent me a Figma link on a Monday morning.

“I did the whole app over the weekend with AI. Can you just polish it?”

Forty screens. Clean spacing. Nice gradients. Honestly, it looked better than a lot of first drafts I’ve seen from people.

Then I asked him one question: “What should a new user do first?”

He scrolled for a while. He couldn’t point to it. Neither could the app.

Making screens is no longer the hard part

This is the shift nobody really talks about. AI didn’t make design easy. It made making things easy.

You can now produce a hundred good-looking screens before lunch. What you can’t produce that fast is the judgement behind them: which ten screens actually matter, what to cut, what your users don’t trust yet, and what will fall apart when a real person with a slow phone and a full inbox tries to use it.

“When everyone can make something that looks finished, deciding what it should be becomes the real work.”

designing-trust-into-savings.linkedin:
Ten minutes into a research call, a woman stopped answering my questions and started telling me a story.

Years ago she’d joined a savings group with people she trusted. One day the person holding the money stopped picking up calls.

“So,” she said, “why would I trust an app?”

I didn’t have an answer. That was the moment the KOYNX project changed for me.

People had heard every promise already

Almost everyone we spoke to had a version of that story. A group that collapsed. An app that suddenly froze withdrawals. A friend who “would pay back next month.”

Big words like “secure” and “guaranteed” didn’t calm anyone down. They’d heard all of that before.

“Trust isn’t something you say. It’s something people can check, again and again, without asking you.”

So we stopped promising and started showing

→ Put the boring details right where people look: when the money unlocks, and what happens if you need it early.
→ Let group members see who has paid this round, so nobody has to chase anyone.
→ Show the name on the receiving account before the PIN, so there’s no doubt about where money is going.

None of these were exciting to design. All of them came straight from people’s fears.

What I took away

Next time you start a fintech project, ask people about money they’ve lost, not just money they want to save.

Their answers will show you exactly which screens need to work hardest.

tokens-first.linkedin:
Three products. One small team. One deadline that didn’t care about either.

I did what felt natural: I designed the components first. Buttons, cards, inputs. Beautiful ones.

Then the admin dashboard needed tighter tables. The mobile app needed bigger tap areas. Every “small exception” created a new version of something.

Within a few weeks the system wasn’t a system. It was a collection.

The fix was making decisions before shapes

I went back and started with tokens: the small, named decisions underneath everything. Which colour means “do this.” How much space sits between related things. How big a heading is.

Each product could then use those same decisions at its own size. Same language, different density.

“If a developer has to ask which grey to use, the system has already let them down.”

Two mistakes I won’t repeat

→ Naming things by how they look (“blue-500”) instead of what they do (“action-primary”). One brand change meant editing hundreds of layers.
→ Writing the documentation in a separate file nobody opened. Notes inside the components did more than any handbook.

If you’re starting a system this month, start smaller than feels right. Ten good decisions beat a hundred pretty components.

I’ve “started learning to code” more times than I’d like to admit.

A bit of C years ago. Some terminal commands. Tutorials I finished without really understanding.

This time I made one rule: only build things I designed myself. If I write a line of code, I should know exactly why it’s there.

The first thing code taught me had nothing to do with code

In Figma, a screen is a picture. In code, a screen is the result of some information: who the user is, what they’ve done, what’s still loading.

That one line showed me two screens I had never drawn. The waiting one, and the empty one.

“Learning to code didn’t make me less of a designer. It showed me which parts of my designs were just wishful thinking.”

What I do differently now

→ Design the loading, empty and error screens next to the main one, not later.
→ Name layers the way a developer would name things.
→ Put rough work on a live link early, even when it’s embarrassing.

If you’re a designer thinking about learning to code: start with something you already designed. It hits differently.

rebrand-without-erasing-history.linkedin:
When people hear “rebrand,” they picture a shiny new logo.

When I started working on a college’s brand, my first job was the opposite. I had to figure out what people would be upset to lose.

A school brand belongs to a lot of people

Former students remember the colours from their uniform. Parents remember the fees page. Current students mostly remember whether the portal let them log in.

A brand refresh that only pleases the marketing team won’t last a semester.

So I went looking for what was already working

I collected everything: signs, social posts, the website, printed forms, the student portal. The name and colours were genuinely recognised. That was worth protecting.

What felt tired was everything around them: too many fonts, random icons, and a homepage trying to say ten things at once.

→ Kept the colours, but gave them clear rules.
→ Went from four fonts to one family.
→ Gave announcements a proper home, so admission news stops taking over everything.

“A good refresh makes people think “they got their act together,” not “who is this?””

My test was simple: can a former student recognise the college’s post in their feed before reading the name? If yes, we kept what mattered.

onboarding-five-people.linkedin:
For WeMove, a fitness app, I designed an onboarding I was genuinely proud of.

Eight thoughtful questions. Clean layout. Friendly copy.

Then I watched five real people use it.

By question four, everyone was tapping “Skip” without reading. One person said, “I just want to see a workout.”

Why I test with five people, not fifty

Five people won’t tell you everything. But they’ll show you the biggest problem almost immediately, and that’s what you need first.

→ Find five people who actually match your users, not your colleagues.
→ Give one simple task: “Set this up so it’s useful to you.”
→ Watch. Say nothing. The awkward silences are where the lessons are.
→ Fix the top three problems, then do it again.

“Testing isn’t about proving your design works. It’s about finding out where it doesn’t, as early and cheaply as possible.”

We cut onboarding down to three questions and moved the rest into the first week of using the app. The one question we kept up front was the one that mattered most: how active are you right now?

logo-is-not-brand.linkedin:
Nearly every new brand enquiry I get starts the same way.

“I need a logo.”

After years of freelance work, I now reply with a question: where will people actually see your business this month?

The answer is usually a WhatsApp status, a few Instagram posts, a flyer and maybe a shop sign.

The logo isn’t what makes those work

It helps. But what makes people remember you is seeing the same colours, the same tone and the same feel everywhere they meet you.

What I suggest starting with instead

→ One sentence that says what you do and who it’s for.
→ Two brand colours and one neutral. Used every single time.
→ One font for headings, one for everything else.
→ Three ready-to-use templates: a post, a status and a flyer.
→ Then the logo, designed to sit comfortably inside all of that.

“Consistency beats cleverness. A simple mark used everywhere does more than a brilliant one used once.”

If you’re a small business owner reading this, look at your last five posts side by side. Do they look like they came from the same business?

naming-components.linkedin:
Halfway through a build, my developer sent me a message.

“Quick one. Is Card/Large the same as Tile/Primary?”

They were the same thing. I’d just named them on different days, in different moods.

That question cost us an afternoon. Multiply it across a project and you lose weeks.

Names are the cheapest documentation you’ll ever write

→ Name things by their job, not their look: “PaymentSummary,” not “BlueCard.”
→ Agree on one word with your developer and use it in both Figma and code.
→ Use variants for state and size: default, pressed, disabled; small, medium, large.
→ If a name needs explaining, it’s the wrong name.

“A design system is a shared language. The names are its vocabulary.”

After one afternoon of renaming, the questions almost stopped. Even better, my developer started suggesting names in the comments. That’s when you know you’re speaking the same language.

design-for-states.linkedin:
In Figma, my little web app had five screens. All of them looked perfect.

Then I opened it on my phone, on a normal Abuja network, and watched it struggle.

Half-loaded images. A blank white screen for four seconds. A button I tapped twice because nothing seemed to happen.

The screens nobody designs

→ Offline: what still works, and how do you say so without scaring anyone?
→ Slow: a grey outline of the page feels faster than a spinning circle.
→ Half-loaded: the text arrived, but one image didn’t.
→ First visit vs. returning: the same screen with two very different jobs.

“A design isn’t finished when it looks right. It’s finished when it still feels right on a bad connection.”

Now I draw the empty, loading and error screens beside every main screen, before I call anything done.

That’s the real reason I want to become a design engineer. Not to replace developers, but to hand them designs that already know how they’ll be used.
